message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (usually not more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or unlawful entry. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and request a written notice if you suspect improper entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a **written notice** of termination. | • Keep copies of all notices and confirm receipt. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord, keep receipts, and calculate the deduction. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (7 days) or a **Notice to Vacate** (30 days) for non‑payment or lease violations.
• Eviction must be filed in court; the landlord cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond to notices promptly, attend court hearings, and keep all documentation. | | **Fair Housing** | • You have the right to fair housing under federal and state law. | • Report violations to HUD or TCHR. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If utilities are included, the landlord must maintain them. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide insurance for your personal property. | • Consider renter’s insurance for protection. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for damages, recover unpaid rent, or seek an injunction to stop unlawful actions. | • Consult an attorney or a tenant advocacy group. | #### Quick Tips for Protecting Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Understand all terms, especially those about deposits, repairs, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of emails, texts, and written notices. Take photos of any damage or maintenance issues. 3. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or certified mail so you have a record. 4. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific time frames for notice, repairs, and deposit returns. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you encounter a problem, contact the TDHCA, TCHR, or a local tenant rights organization before it escalates. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy group.
